home.headline: Components that compile straight to Vapor, not around it.
home.tagline: 60+ components for Vue 3, compiled from one source to both the classic VDOM build and Vue Vapor.
home.featureVaporTitle: Real Vapor build, not a shim
home.featureVaporBody: Every component compiles through Vue 3.6's Vapor mode from the same source.
home.featureAnimationBody: Plain CSS by default, or drive it yourself with GSAP or motion-v.
home.featureI18nBody: Every built-in string translates through your own i18n instance.
home.featurePrimitivesBody: No compound-component sprawl and no hidden context to wire up.
home.featureSsrBody: Every component checks for a real browser before it touches window or document. It renders safely in Nuxt, server-rendered apps, and static site generators. This docs site is built with Vite SSG from the same components.
home.featureSkillBody: A companion package that teaches Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, and other agents every component's real API. It's generated from the library's own types, not written by hand.
home.newText: 0.5.0: spring folds, a color picker, inline editing

gettingStarted.title: Getting started
gettingStarted.intro: A Vue 3 component library with a full Vue Vapor build. Animations use plain CSS by default, or you can bring your own animation library.
gettingStarted.vaporIntro: Both builds ship from the same package and source, with the same props. Pick the one your app runs. Every component page has a toggle to compare them.
gettingStarted.vaporPinIntro: The Vapor build needs Vue 3.6, which is still a prerelease. Install the exact version vael-ui is built against, {version}. A range such as ^3.5.0 can install Vue 3.5, which has no Vapor mode, and a different prerelease can break the compiled components:
gettingStarted.vaporAppIntro: A Vapor app starts with createVaporApp and imports components, composables and directives from 'vael-ui/vapor'. Your own components opt in with <script setup vapor>:
gettingStarted.vaporForceIntro: To skip the vapor attribute in every file, turn on features.vapor in {'@'}vitejs/plugin-vue 6.0.8 or later. Every <script setup> component in your app then compiles as Vapor:
gettingStarted.vaporMixIntro: A classic app can also host Vapor components. This helps when you move an existing app to Vapor a few components at a time. Keep createApp, install Vue's vaporInteropPlugin, and import from 'vael-ui/vapor' in the components you mark vapor. For a new app, pick one build instead. A component marked vapor also imports directives such as vTooltip from 'vael-ui/vapor' itself, because a directive registered with app.directive only reaches classic components.
gettingStarted.installIntro: vael-ui is on npm. Install it with your package manager:
gettingStarted.usageImportNote: Each component imports its own styles. Add this import only if you're on a version before 0.2.0 or want all styles loaded at once. See {link} for base-style setup.
gettingStarted.usageIntro: Then import components from 'vael-ui' for the classic VDOM build. For the Vapor build (Vue 3.6's mode without a virtual DOM), import from 'vael-ui/vapor'. The props are the same in both:
gettingStarted.fontIntro: Components use the font of the page around them and ship no font of their own. Without one, the browser falls back to its default serif font, so set a font on body:
gettingStarted.darkModeIntro: Dark mode is CSS-only. It follows <html data-theme="dark"> and falls back to prefers-color-scheme. vael-ui ships no toggle UI. useColorScheme() tracks OS-preference changes and saves the choice through the persist option you pass:
gettingStarted.appearanceHeadIntro: If you save color mode or app-wide font size in localStorage, place this script in your HTML <head> before the app bundle. It restores both before paint. Save a CSS font size such as 13px or 1rem under app-font-size. Components inherit it unless you set a scoped theme.fontSize.
gettingStarted.directivesIntro: v-tooltip and v-scroll-mask aren't registered globally by default. If you use either one in more than one component, register them once:
gettingStarted.directivesNote: v-tooltip also needs one <TooltipHost /> mounted in your app. In a Vapor app, import both directives from vael-ui/vapor instead.
gettingStarted.ssrIntro: Both builds render on the server and hydrate in the browser. {link} sets up everything below for you.
gettingStarted.ssrNoExternal: With plain Vite SSR, let Vite bundle vael-ui for the server. Each component imports its own CSS, and Node can't load CSS files on its own:
gettingStarted.ssrTeleports: Dialogs, popovers, toasts and tooltips render into <body> through <Teleport>. Vue returns that HTML separately in ctx.teleports. Add it at the start of <body>, before your app's element, or the page won't hydrate cleanly:
gettingStarted.ssrLocale: Set locale on ConfigProvider when you render on a server. Without it, dates, numbers and the first day of the week follow the server's language, then change once the page runs in the browser.

globalSetup.title: Global setup
globalSetup.intro: vael-ui has four singletons. Mount each one once, anywhere in your app, and every component that needs it finds it.
globalSetup.tooltipHostIntro: Renders every v-tooltip. If it isn't mounted, tooltips never appear and no error is shown.
globalSetup.tooltipHostOptions: It takes the same options that each tooltip can override:
globalSetup.dialogHostIntro: Renders dialogs opened from code by openDialog() or confirmAction(). You don't need it for a <Dialog v-model:open> in your own template. It has no props or configuration.
globalSetup.popoverHostIntro: Renders popovers opened from code by openPopover(), or by confirmAction() with surface: 'popover'. You don't need it for a <Popover v-model:open> in your own template. It has no props or configuration.
globalSetup.toasterIntro: Renders the toasts that {code} creates. It has its own props, so it's documented on {link}.
globalSetup.allTogetherIntro: Mount all four once, in your app's root template:

tailwind.layerNote: vael-ui ships in {layer}. Tailwind v4 also puts its utilities in a layer, so import order matters. Import vael-ui's CSS before your Tailwind entry (shown below) so its layer registers first. Tailwind's utilities layer then comes after it in the cascade, and a Tailwind utility on a vael-ui component always wins. You don't need {important} or specificity fights. See {link} for how layers work.
tailwind.orderWarning: Each component loads its own CSS, so you don't import a stylesheet for vael-ui. Tailwind v4 is the one exception. Its utilities live in their own cascade layer, and the first stylesheet to name a layer sets the order. Import vael-ui/layers.css before your Tailwind entry, in your app's main entry file. It only names vael-ui's layer and loads no component CSS, so the order holds as components load their CSS later.
tailwind.mergingIntro: Every component takes a ui prop for part classes (for example :ui="{'{'} root: 'my-class' {'}'}"). To resolve conflicting Tailwind utilities there the way tailwind-merge does (the last one wins per property), set it up once:
tailwind.mergingNote: Every ui.* part class in the tree now goes through twMerge.

stylingLayers.title: Styling and cascade layers
stylingLayers.intro: vael-ui ships in {layer}. Unlayered CSS always beats layered CSS, whatever its specificity. So a plain, unlayered base reset overrides vael-ui's internal styles without any warning. To fix this, put your base styles in a layer too, and order that layer first.
stylingLayers.orderNote: Here, import order only sets the layer position. An unlayered override always wins, wherever it loads.
stylingLayers.bundlerNote: Each component imports its own styles. Add the import below only if you're on a version before 0.2.0 or want all styles loaded at once.
stylingLayers.overrideNote: When you override one component on purpose (with the {code} prop or a Tailwind utility), you want your rule to win. Keep that CSS unlayered, which it is by default. See {link}.
stylingLayers.cssVariablesIntro: Every color, radius, shadow, and motion value in vael-ui comes from a CSS custom property. Override any of them in your own unlayered stylesheet:
stylingLayers.cssVariablesThemeNote: ConfigProvider's theme sets primary, danger, radius and fontSize. Without fontSize, components follow your html font size, form fields included. If that's under 16px, call preventFocusZoom() once so iPhones don't zoom into fields. Set other tokens with CSS.

rows.primary: Primary action color (buttons, links, focus accents).
rows.primaryHover: Hover state for the primary color.
rows.primaryContrast: Text/icon color on top of the primary color.
rows.contrastVariant: Text/icon color on top of this color.
rows.surface: Base background for panels, cards, and dialogs.
rows.borderStrong: Stronger border color for emphasized edges.
rows.overlay: Backdrop color behind modals and dialogs.
rows.radius: Base corner radius for controls (buttons, inputs, badges).
rows.radiusSurface: Capped corner radius for large surfaces (panels, cards, tables), so a large radius setting can't turn them into pill shapes.
rows.zPopover: Stacking order for popovers, menus, and selects.
rows.toastOffset: Edge offset for the toast stack.
rows.joinFrame: On your control's bordered element, not on Field. Optional value: sm, md or lg.
rows.joinStart: A cell or an attached label sits on the control's start edge.
rows.joinEnd: A cell or an attached label sits on the control's end edge.
rows.joinAttached: Field draws the label as a joined cell.
rows.cellBg: Background of joined cells: an attached label, #prepend and #append.
rows.labelWidth: Width of a start/end label. Set it on a parent to line up a whole form.

stylingLayers.joinTitle: Joining your own control to a Field
stylingLayers.joinIntro: A Field's attached label and #prepend/#append cells join the control's bordered frame. vael-ui's own controls mark that frame with data-ui-frame. Add the same attribute to your own control and it joins too. Give it the control's size (sm, md or lg) and the cells match its corner radius and font size.
stylingLayers.joinLayerNote: Field's join rules are in {layer}, so if your control's own styles are unlayered, they win. In that case, flatten the corners and recolor the border yourself with the attributes Field sets on its root:
stylingLayers.joinCellNote: Give a control inside a cell its own aria-label. It stands alone, so the Field's label doesn't name it.
stylingLayers.advancedNote: You won't need this for everyday use. It's for building your own controls that plug into vael-ui.

animation.title: Bring your own animation
animation.intro: Every component that animates ships a plain CSS transition, and each one lets you take over: drive it with GSAP, motion-v, or nothing at all. Which hooks you get depends on what the component does.
animation.motionCssIntro: Set it to false to turn off the built-in CSS transition. The component still changes state, but instantly, and leaves the DOM for you to animate. On a ConfigProvider, :motion-css="false" means no animation at all: everything inside opens, closes and leaves instantly, with nothing for you to handle.
animation.forceMountIntro: Keeps content mounted while closed, instead of removing it with v-if, and turns off the built-in transition. Animate the exposed panelEl as it opens, and pair it with beforeClose(done) to run your own exit.
animation.beforeCloseIntro: For imperative libraries: pass a function that receives done. The component stays mounted, with isClosing set, until you call it.
animation.motionVExampleIntro: forceMount hands you the panel. Animate panelEl in when it opens, and run the exit in beforeClose(done), which keeps the panel up until you call done():
animation.gsapExampleIntro: beforeClose(done) plus the exposed panelEl ref, so the tween runs on the real panel element before it's removed:
animation.kindsTitle: Hooks for each kind of component
animation.kindsCheck: A component's Props, Slots and Exposed tables list exactly what it has.
animation.exposedIntro: Put a template ref on a component and you get its real DOM elements: el for the root, plus its parts, like panelEl, listEl, thumbEl or checkEl. Turn the built-in transition off with motionCss and animate those elements with any library. Each component's Exposed table lists what it has.
animation.exposedExampleIntro: In this example, the check mark pops in with GSAP each time the box is checked:

descriptions.ConfigProvider: Wraps your app to provide theming, i18n, and class merging to every component inside it.
descriptions.Button: A clickable action with variants, sizes, loading states, and icon slots built in.
descriptions.SplitButton: A primary action fused with a chevron that opens alternate actions in a dropdown.
descriptions.Toolbar: A horizontal strip for grouping related actions, with roving keyboard focus.
descriptions.SpeedDial: A floating action button that fans out into secondary actions on demand.
descriptions.Dial: A circular drag control for picking a numeric value, like a volume knob.
descriptions.SelectButton: A segmented control for choosing one or more values from a short list.
descriptions.Input: A single-line text field with sizes, states, and slots for icons or hints.
descriptions.Textarea: A multi-line text field that can auto-grow with its content.
descriptions.InputNumber: A numeric field with increment and decrement controls and format-aware parsing.
descriptions.OtpInput: A row of single-character boxes for one-time codes, with paste and auto-advance.
descriptions.Editable: Text that turns into an input when clicked and saves on Enter or blur, for renaming in place.
descriptions.ColorPicker: A color swatch that opens a picker: a saturation and brightness plane, a hue slider, a hex field, an eyedropper where the browser has one, and optional presets.
descriptions.PasswordInput: A password field with a reveal toggle and a requirements hint.
descriptions.Checkbox: A checkbox for a single yes/no choice, with an optional indeterminate state.
descriptions.Radio: One option in a mutually exclusive set. Always use it inside a RadioGroup.
descriptions.RadioGroup: Groups a set of Radio buttons so only one can be selected at a time.
descriptions.Switch: An on/off toggle styled like a physical switch, for immediate-effect settings.
descriptions.Slider: Drag a handle (or two, for a range) along a track to pick a numeric value.
descriptions.Knob: A rotary control for picking a numeric value within a fixed arc.
descriptions.Field: Wraps a form control with a label, help text, and error message, wired together for you.
descriptions.DatePicker: A text field paired with a calendar popover for picking a date or range.
descriptions.Calendar: A month grid for picking a single date or a date range.
descriptions.FileUpload: A drop zone and file list for picking files, with validation.
descriptions.Rating: Click, drag, or use arrow keys to pick a value on a row of stars, with optional half-step precision.
descriptions.Select: A dropdown for picking one or more values from a list, with filtering and virtualization.
descriptions.Combobox: A searchable dropdown that also accepts free text, so autocomplete and tagging are one component.
descriptions.CascadeSelect: A dropdown for picking a path through nested options, one level at a time.
descriptions.Tree: A collapsible, indented list for hierarchical data, with single or multiple selection.
descriptions.TreeSelect: A dropdown whose panel is a Tree, for picking one or more nodes from a hierarchy.
descriptions.Dialog: A modal overlay that blocks the page until someone responds or dismisses it.
descriptions.Drawer: A panel that slides in from a viewport edge, for navigation or side content.
descriptions.Popover: A floating panel anchored to a trigger element, for menus, forms, or extra detail.
descriptions.Tooltip: A small floating label that appears on hover or focus to explain an element.
descriptions.BottomSheet: A panel that slides up from the bottom edge, for touch layouts.
descriptions.ContextMenu: A menu that opens at the pointer on right-click, replacing the native browser menu.
descriptions.Tour: A guided walkthrough that highlights one element at a time next to a callout, for onboarding and product tours.
descriptions.Menu: A dropdown list of actions opened from a trigger, with full keyboard navigation.
descriptions.MenuList: Menu's rows rendered in the page flow instead of a dropdown, for a permanent sidebar nav.
descriptions.Tabs: Switches between panels of content, with a sliding indicator under the active tab.
descriptions.Toaster: Renders the notifications that toast() creates. Mount it once, anywhere in your app.
descriptions.Message: An inline banner for status text: info, success, warning, or error.
descriptions.Progress: A progress bar for a task or stacked shares of a whole, with determinate and indeterminate states and an optional legend.
descriptions.Loader: A small spinner that shows something is in progress.
descriptions.Skeleton: A placeholder shape that stands in for content while it loads.
descriptions.DataTable: A data grid with sorting, selection, column resizing, and virtualization, built from Column components.
descriptions.Column: Defines one column of a DataTable. Always use it inside a DataTable.
descriptions.Pagination: Page-number controls for splitting a long list or table across pages.
descriptions.Card: A bordered container for grouping related content, with optional title and actions.
descriptions.Avatar: A circular or square image or initials that represents a person or entity.
descriptions.Badge: A small dot, count, or label overlaid on the corner of another element.
descriptions.Tag: A compact label for categorizing or annotating an item inline.
descriptions.Chip: A removable, compact token for selected filters, tags, or multi-select values.
descriptions.Kbd: Styles a keyboard shortcut so it reads like a physical key.
descriptions.Timeline: An ordered list of steps joined by a line. Each step can hold any content.
descriptions.Accordion: A stack of collapsible sections where opening one can close the others.
descriptions.AccordionItem: One collapsible section of an Accordion. Always use it inside an Accordion.
descriptions.Collapsible: A single show/hide section for optional or secondary content.
descriptions.Separator: A thin line, with an optional label, that divides content into groups.
descriptions.Resizable: A drag handle that resizes a panel between a minimum and maximum size.
descriptions.SwipeToReveal: Swipe an item to reveal actions underneath it, like a native mobile list row.
descriptions.Sortable: A drag-to-reorder list that also works from the keyboard, not only with a pointer.
descriptions.PullToRefresh: A pull-down gesture at the top of a scroll container that triggers a refresh.
descriptions.Dock: A macOS-style row of icons that magnify as the pointer approaches them.
descriptions.BreadcrumbItem: One link or the current page in a Breadcrumb trail.
descriptions.BreadcrumbSeparator: The divider between two BreadcrumbItems. It shows a chevron unless you pass your own content.
descriptions.ButtonGroup: Joins buttons into one connected row or column, and can turn them into single or multiple toggles.
descriptions.CommandPalette: A searchable list of commands in a dialog, opened from a button or a keyboard shortcut such as ⌘K.
descriptions.Stepper: Shows progress through a sequence of steps, and lets people move between them.
descriptions.Breadcrumb: A trail of links from the top of the site down to the current page.
descriptions.AvatarGroup: Stacks several avatars into one overlapping row, with a count for the ones that don’t fit.
descriptions.ScrollArea: A scroll box with slim, themed scrollbars and faded edges, in one or both directions.

pageNotes.Resizable: This site's own sidebar is built with Resizable. Drag its right edge to try it.
pageNotes.ContextMenu: Keyboard users open the menu with Shift+F10 or the Menu key, which fire contextmenu on the focused element, so make the wrapped target focusable (tabindex="0") and give it an accessible name.
pageNotes.Tree: Rows update from reactive state, so a custom #node slot should read reactive values (props, refs, computeds), not plain variables captured from the parent.
pageNotes.DataTable: Big tables: with hundreds of rows, add virtualize and a scroll-height, for example scroll-height="400px". The table then draws only the rows in view, so sorting, selecting and scrolling stay fast. When more than 150 rows are on screen at once, rows also stop sliding into place as they sort.

i18nKeys.title: Translating vael-ui
i18nKeys.intro: Every built-in string (the dialog close button, toast dismiss, empty states, and so on) has an English default. To translate them, pass your own i18n instance to ConfigProvider. It reads from your existing catalog under the uiKit namespace, so there's nothing extra to install. Keys you haven't translated keep the English default, with no console warnings.
i18nKeys.copyIntro: Copy this into your locale files under the uiKit key, then translate the values:

autoImport.title: Auto import
autoImport.intro: vael-ui/resolver is a resolver for unplugin-vue-components. Register it once, and you can use any vael-ui component in a template without importing it.
autoImport.setupIntro: Add the resolver wherever unplugin-vue-components is already configured:
autoImport.setupOutro: Write the tag, and the plugin adds the import at build time:
autoImport.vaporIntro: vael-ui ships two builds from the same source: the regular VDOM build and a Vapor build (vael-ui/vapor). The resolver imports from the VDOM build by default. Pass variant: 'vapor' to import from the Vapor build instead. The resolver imports every component from one build, so pick the one your app renders with.
autoImport.vaporHostsNote: In a Vapor template, unplugin-vue-components only finds components that sit inside another component's slot. Import top-level ones by hand, such as <Toaster>, <DialogHost> and <ConfigProvider>, until unplugin-vue-components supports Vapor.
autoImport.oneImportIntro: Your editor's auto-import may keep suggesting vael-ui instead of vael-ui/vapor. This is a known TypeScript limitation when a package exports the same name from two entry points. To avoid it, set a vapor export condition instead of importing from the subpath. Every import … from 'vael-ui' then resolves to the Vapor build across the project, for components and composables alike. Auto-import has nothing left to get wrong.
autoImport.oneImportDefaults: Add vapor to Vite's default conditions instead of replacing them. A bare ['vapor'] drops the defaults, and other packages can then load the wrong file. The ssr line does the same for server rendering.
autoImport.oneImportNote: The Vite condition controls which build loads. The TS condition keeps the types in line with it. If you set one without the other, you get a silent mismatch instead of an error: correct types with the wrong build loaded, or the reverse.
autoImport.cssIntro: No extra setup here. Every vael-ui component imports its own CSS, so resolving a component also loads its styles. Most unplugin-vue-components resolvers need a separate sideEffects entry for that.
autoImport.bundlersIntro: unplugin-vue-components supports Vite, Webpack, Rollup, esbuild, and Rspack. The resolver is a plain function, so it works the same with all of them.

nuxt.title: Nuxt
nuxt.intro: vael-ui/nuxt is a Nuxt module. Add it once, and you can use any vael-ui component in a template without importing it. It uses Nuxt's built-in component registration, not unplugin-vue-components.
nuxt.setupIntro: Register the module in your Nuxt config:
nuxt.setupOutro: Write the tag, and Nuxt resolves the import for you:
nuxt.appSetupIntro: The module registers components only. Mount the hosts you use once in app.vue. {link} explains what each one does.
nuxt.composablesIntro: Composables such as toast() and openDialog() aren't auto-imported. Import them from 'vael-ui', or from 'vael-ui/vapor' with the Vapor variant:
nuxt.directivesIntro: The v-tooltip and v-scroll-mask directives aren't registered either. Register them in a plugin. With the Vapor variant, import them from 'vael-ui/vapor':
nuxt.excludeIntro: Skip specific component names, for example to register your own <Button> under the same tag:
nuxt.vaporIntro: Set variant: 'vapor' to use vael-ui/vapor, the same option vael-ui/resolver takes. The module turns on Nuxt's vue.vapor for you. It needs Nuxt 4.6 or later and Vue 3.6. Pin Vue to the exact version given in Getting started.
nuxt.vaporOutro: Pages still render on the server. The server turns each component into HTML, and the browser picks it up as a Vapor component, with nothing else to configure.
nuxt.vaporForceIntro: To compile your own <script setup> components as Vapor too, without adding vapor to each one, turn on {'@'}vitejs/plugin-vue's features.vapor through Nuxt's vite.vue:
nuxt.resolverIntro: If your Nuxt app already uses unplugin-vue-components to auto-import other libraries, use vael-ui/resolver instead. See the {link} guide.

skill.title: AI agent skill
skill.intro: A companion package that teaches AI coding agents how to use vael-ui. It works with Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, Cursor, and others. It covers every component's props, slots, and events, every composable, and how to set up animation, theming, and the VDOM/Vapor split. It's generated from the library's own types and docs content, not written by hand, so it stays accurate as the library changes. It's versioned and released separately from vael-ui.
skill.claudeCodeIntro: Add the marketplace once, then install the skill:
skill.otherAgentsIntro: Any agent that supports the shared Agent Skills spec can install it with skill.sh. That includes GitHub Copilot, Codex, Cursor, and more than 70 others:
skill.whatsIncludedIntro: A compact top-level guide and a full reference, generated from the same data as this docs site:
skill.includedComponents: Every component's props, slots, events, and exposed refs
skill.includedComposables: Every standalone composable's parameters, return values, and usage examples
skill.includedAnimation: The animation-agnostic contract (motionCss, forceMount, beforeClose), with real GSAP and motion-v examples
skill.includedStyling: Cascade layer ordering and the full CSS variable reference for theming
skill.sourceIntro: The skill's source lives at {link}, along with instructions for updating it outside vael-ui's release cycle.

notFound.title: Page not found
notFound.body: The page you're looking for doesn't exist or has moved.

composableDescriptions.confirmAction: An async-aware confirm flow, shown as a centered dialog or a popover anchored to a trigger. It waits for your handler before closing.
composableDescriptions.useDialogService: Opens any component as a dialog from code instead of markup. It returns a promise that resolves with the value the dialog closes with.
composableDescriptions.usePopoverService: Opens any component as an anchored popover from code instead of markup. It returns a promise that resolves with the value the popover closes with.
composableDescriptions.useToast: Shows toast notifications from anywhere in your app, with variant shortcuts and a promise helper that swaps a loading toast for success or error.
composableDescriptions.useTour: The headless state machine behind Tour: step and group navigation, with no DOM or rendering built in.
composableDescriptions.useAsyncLoading: Tracks every pending promise you pass it, so a loading state clears only once all of them have settled.
composableDescriptions.useNumberFormat: Locale-aware number formatting and parsing that stay in sync, so typed text and its formatted display always match.
composableDescriptions.useColorScheme: Switches between light, dark, and system theme modes. Persistence is optional, through storage functions you provide.
composableDescriptions.preventFocusZoom: Stops iOS zooming into form fields, so they can match the rest of your text size.
composableDescriptions.useFloatingPosition: The positioning engine behind Popover, Menu, and Tooltip, built on Floating UI. Use it to build your own anchored surfaces.
composableDescriptions.useVirtualizer: Windowed rendering for long lists, so only the visible rows exist in the DOM.
composableDescriptions.useFieldControl: Connects a custom form control to the nearest Field: id, ARIA attributes, and focus and filled state.

dockTour.settingsDescription: Along with the theme color, corner radius, size, font size, language and more.
dockTour.searchDescription: Find any component, guide or composable by name, with a short description of each.
